readerTitle: The rival your scorecard tells you to ignore
caseNote: 가상 사례 (피자 가게, 회계 소프트웨어) + 실제 연구 (Christensen의 디스크 드라이브 연구, 2015년 HBR의 Uber 분석) · 피자·소프트웨어 수치는 모두 설명용
insight: 변화가 파괴적인지는 기술이 얼마나 새로운지가 아니라, 내 핵심 고객의 평가 기준에서 이기는지 지는지로 판단한다.
misconception: 기술이 획기적이거나 화제가 크면 파괴적 혁신이다. 내 기준에서 품질이 낮은 경쟁자는 위협이 아니다.

sources.text: Christensen, C. M. (1997). The Innovator's Dilemma. Harvard Business School Press.
Bower, J. L. & Christensen, C. M. (1995). Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave. Harvard Business Review.
Christensen, C. M., Raynor, M. & McDonald, R. (2015). What Is Disruptive Innovation? Harvard Business Review.
피자 가게와 회계 소프트웨어의 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 디스크 드라이브 연구: 기존 업체는 기술적으로 어려운 것을 포함한 존속적 개선을 주도했고, 처음에는 용량이 작은 소형 드라이브(예: 8인치 → 5.25인치)에서 신규 업체에 밀렸다는 요지. 소형 드라이브의 첫 고객이 '더 작은 컴퓨터 제조사'(데스크톱 PC 등)였다는 표현을 원문으로 다시 확인하세요.
Uber: Christensen 외(2015)는 Uber가 저가 시장이나 비소비자 시장이 아니라 주류 고객에게서 출발했으므로 이론상 파괴적 혁신에 맞지 않는다고 주장했습니다. 카드에는 '저자들의 주장'으로만 적었습니다. 출처 문구를 확인하세요.
피자 가게 차트 수치(맛 8/9/6점, 40/45/5분, $24/$30/$6)와 '맛 점수가 6점에서 7점으로 오르면'이라는 경로는 모두 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 계산이 필요한 부분은 없고, 7점이 '단골이 받아들일 수준'이라는 것도 가정입니다.

cards.title: Two rivals open near your pizzeria.
body: You run a sit-down pizzeria with loyal regulars. This spring, two new places open nearby.
One imported a wood-fired oven and hired a well-known chef. The other is a slice counter at the train station: reheated slices, no seats, five minutes from order to out the door.
Only one of them is playing your game.

image.label: A fancy pizzeria and a tiny station slice counter facing each other
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에는 장작 화덕과 테이블이 있는 고급 피자 가게, 오른쪽에는 역 출구 옆 작은 조각 피자 카운터와 바쁘게 지나가는 통근객들. 가운데에 작은 동네 피자 가게. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which rival should worry you more?
body: Both are new and both sell pizza. You have time to watch only one closely this year.

options.text: The gourmet place. Its pizza is better than yours
options.feedback: It's a real fight, but a familiar one. It wants your customers on your terms, so you already know how to respond.

options.text: The slice counter. It wins on things you don't measure
options.feedback: It looks weak by every measure you use. That is exactly why it's easy to ignore while it grows. The next card shows the numbers.
Loyalty helps against both, but it's a feeling, not a plan. It tells you nothing about which rival is changing the game.

cards.title: On your scorecard, the slice counter loses.
body: Your regulars judge you on taste and a good evening out. Here's how all three score.
cards.callout: The gourmet rival beats you on your measure. The slice counter beats you on measures you never tracked, for commuters you never served.

cards.title: Sustaining vs disruptive change
body: A **sustaining change** makes a product better at what the best customers already value: tastier, faster, more features. The gourmet rival is sustaining.

A **disruptive change** starts out worse on those measures but wins on others, often price, speed or simplicity. It serves people the leaders overlook, then improves until it's good enough for the mainstream.
The test isn't how new the technology is. It's which scorecard the change wins on.

image.label: Two arrows: one climbing the existing scale, one starting low on a new scale
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 축은 "What your customers value". 파란 화살표 "Sustaining"는 이 축 위에서 더 높이 올라감. 주황 화살표 "Disruptive"는 같은 축 아래쪽에서 시작하지만 옆의 다른 축 "Price, speed, simplicity"에서는 높음. 단순한 선과 라벨만 사용.

cards.title: Leaders usually win the fights they recognize.
body: Clayton Christensen studied the computer disk drive industry over many years. Established makers usually led sustaining improvements, even technically difficult ones, because their best customers asked for them.

They stumbled when **smaller drives that held less data** appeared. Their big customers didn't want them, so the leaders held back. New companies sold them to makers of smaller computers, kept improving, and later moved up into the leaders' market.

cards.title: Big news isn't the test.
body: Uber felt like an earthquake for taxis. Yet in 2015, Christensen and two co-authors argued it didn't fit the theory: it started with mainstream riders in big cities, offering a service at least as good as a taxi.
Disruption is also **relative**. The slice counter threatens a sit-down pizzeria by changing what counts. To a fast-food chain that already sells speed and price, it's just another rival.

cards.title: Most cheap entrants stay cheap.
body: Many simple, low-price rivals never get good enough for your customers. A slice counter can stay a slice counter for 20 years. Calling everything disruptive is as unhelpful as ignoring everything.
So watch the path, not the launch. If the counter's taste score rises from 6 to 7, and your regulars would accept a 7 for a quick weeknight meal, the gap that protected you is gone.
And don't relax about sustaining rivals. The gourmet place can still take your best tables.

image.label: A rising line approaching a 'good enough' threshold
image.brief: 단순한 선 그래프. 가로 점선 "Good enough for your regulars (7)". 주황 선 "Slice counter"가 6점에서 시작해 해마다 천천히 올라 점선에 닿기 직전. 위쪽에 파란 선 "Your pizzeria (8)"는 평평함.

cards.title: Now it's accounting software.
body: You sell accounting software to mid-size firms. Your team flags three things happening in the market. Which one is disruptive for you?

options.text: A rival launches AI forecasting for large firms, priced above yours
options.feedback: The technology is new, but it competes on what your clients already value: more power. That's a sustaining fight, and you can match it.

options.text: A $5-a-month phone app that only sends invoices, popular with one-person businesses and improving every quarter
options.feedback: It lacks most of your features, so your users dismiss it. It wins on price and simplicity for people you don't serve, and it's climbing toward what your clients need.

options.text: A rival cuts the price of its full product by 20%
options.feedback: Cheaper, yes, but it's the same product for the same customers. That's a price fight inside your game, not a change in the scorecard.

cards.title: Ask which scorecard a change wins on.
body: Sustaining changes win on your customers' measures, and you usually know how to fight them. Disruptive changes lose on those measures and win on others, so they look harmless at first.
**Try it today:** write down the three things your best customers judge you on. Then name one rival that loses on all three. What does it win on?
